ai.glance: Leonardo's monumental mural captures the dramatic moment when Jesus announces one of his apostles will betray him. Its revolutionary use of perspective and psychological depth inaugurated the High Renaissance.

story.receipt: Leonardo's contemporary, mathematician Luca Pacioli: 'It is impossible to imagine the apostles more vividly reacting to the words of the master.' Vasari later noted that Leonardo left Christ's face unfinished, 'not believing it possible to give it the celestial divinity required.'
story.surface_layer: Christ sits at center of a long table, his arms spread in a gesture of resignation after announcing 'One of you will betray me.' The twelve apostles react in clusters of three, their bodies forming a wave of shock radiating outward from Christ's calm center. Judas, third from left, recoils backward clutching his money bag, his face in shadow. The architectural perspective converges precisely on Christ's head, making him the geometric and spiritual focal point. Through the windows behind, a luminous landscape recedes into sfumato haze.
story.type_aesthetic: High Renaissance mural using experimental oil-and-tempera technique on dry plaster (not true fresco). One-point perspective with mathematical precision. Pioneering use of psychological portraiture-each apostle shows a distinct emotional response.
story.core_philosophy: The moment before action reveals character. Leonardo chose not to depict the institution of the Eucharist or the identification of Judas, but the suspended instant when each man must confront his own capacity for betrayal.
story.cultural_context: Commissioned by Duke Ludovico Sforza for the Dominican refectory of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan. The monks would eat their meals beneath this scene of Christ's final meal-a deliberate theological parallel. Leonardo worked on it from 1495-1498, often standing before it for hours without touching his brush, 'composing in his mind,' to the prior's frustration.

observation_details.label: The Perspective
observation_details.value: All perspective lines converge on Christ's right temple. The room extends the actual refectory's architecture, creating an illusion that Christ dines with the monks

observation_details.label: Judas
observation_details.value: Uniquely placed on the same side as Christ and apostles (unlike tradition), but his face falls into shadow and he clutches his payment

observation_details.label: The Hands
observation_details.value: Leonardo choreographed each hand gesture to reveal psychology-Peter's knife, Thomas's pointed finger, John's folded resignation

observation_details.label: Deterioration
observation_details.value: Leonardo's experimental technique began failing within decades. The painting has been restored multiple times and represents perhaps 20% original paint
